full_judgment:
On an application by the petitioner under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure a Rule was issued calling upon opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 11-3-1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 11 of 1984 reversing those dated 15-1-1984 passed by the learned Munsif, Nawabganj allowing Miscellaneous Case No. 84 of 1980 (a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act) should not be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this court might seem fit and proper. 

 7. Being aggrieved by the judgment and order of the learned Munsif, opposite party No. 1 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 11 of 1984 which was ultimately heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Nawabganj who by his impugned judgment and order dated 11-3-1989 allowed the appeal, setting aside the judgment and order of the court below and dismissed the pre-emption petition holding that the case land not being an agricultural land and being a pond in nature petition claiming preemption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not tenable in law and that the case land being a non-agricultural land preemption could have been claimed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act but in that event contiguous land holder had no occasion to claim preemption. 

 9. Mr AHM Obaidul Kabir, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submits that the learned appellate Court committed an error of law in treating the case land to be a non-agricultural land and that pre-emption under section 56 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was legally tenable. It has also been submitted by him that the petitioner being a contiguous land holder of the case land he was entitled to pre-emption of the case land and further that opposite party No. 1 while resisting the claim of pre-emption did not himself submit a separate petition seeking proportionate pre-emption of the case land and that therefore, the learned trial Court rightly allowed pre-emption in favour of the petitioner. In this connection he has cited a decision in the case of Golchera Khatun and others vs Sayer a Khatoon, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 133. 

 13. On the other hand, opposite party No. 1 also claimed co-sharership in the case holding by way of purchase from Abdus Sattar who in his turn purchased 1/3 rd interest of opposite party No. 4 Raisuddin by a kabala dated 13-3-1976. His own deed of purchase which was exhibited by opposite party No. 1 in the trial Court and was received in evidence as exhibit A(1) showed that opposite party No. 1 purchased from Abdus Sattar on 30-1-1980 after accrual of the cause of action for pre-emption in favour of the petitioner on 18-1-1980. So, acquisition of co-sharership by purchase after accrual of cause of action for pre-emption cannot defeat pre-emption. In this connection a decision in the case of Abdul Baten vs Abdul Latif Sheikh and others, reported in 45 DLR (AD) 26 is relevant. It has been held by their Lordships therein "The right of pre-emption accrued to the pre-emptor is not affected by the subsequent acquisition of co- sharership by the pre-emptee". In the present case under revision it is found that opposite party No. 1 acquired such co-sharership in the case holding by purchase after accrual of the cause of action for pre- emption in favour of the petitioner. 

 5. In this case the pre-emptee tried to resist the claim of the pre-emptor and did not join in the application for pre-emption as a transferee co-sharer and did not take any step required under sub-section (4) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to join in the appellant’s application for pre-emption. She cannot be unranked the half of the case land in the name of even handed justice on the ground that both the pre-emptors and the pre-emptee were found being co-sharers by purchase to be on equal footing." 

 "10. Mr BK Das, the learned Advocate, submits that the purchaser pre-emptee who is also the petitioner in the revision petition is not required to file an application for proportional pre-emption under section 96(5)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1951 as the purchaser pre-emptee is not a stranger to the case land but a person holding land contiguous to the case land. He further argues that it is particularly not necessary as the purchaser pre-emptee has already been resisting a pre- emption application. He submits that the purpose of section 96 of the said Act is to disallow strangers from holding land, but the pre-emptee is not a stranger, rather he is an admitted contiguous landowner. Therefore, courts below have erred in law in insisting on an application from him for proportionate pre-emption. I find it difficult to accept this argument as section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is quite clear that intending pre-emptee whether co-sharers by inheritance, co-sharer by purchase or a holder of contiguous land shall have to file a pre-emption application within a specific period of time. By not doing so the pre-emptee, drips Mia, had simply waived his right to pre-empt the case land." 

 Now, the pertinent question is, whether the case land which comprised a tank was to be treated as non-agricultural land. Learned Advocate, for the petitioner in this connection, has drawn my attention to the definition of 'Non-agricultural land" as expressed in section 2(4) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. It has been defined as such: 

 In this connection definition of "land" as given in section 2(16) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is also worthy of consideration. It has been defined as follows: 

 From the aforesaid definition of "Land" a pond which remains covered with water at any time of the year falls within the definition of land including benefits to arise therefrom. In a decision in the case of Sayeda Khatun and another vs Abedur Rahman and others reported in 1986 BLD (AD) 330 it has been held by their Lordships whether a particular land is non-agricultural land is also to be determined with reference to the user thereof. Both the petitioner as PW 1 and opposite party No.1 as OPW 1 admitted in their deposition that both of them had been using the case land comprising a pond for irrigating water to their crop lands which were contiguous to it. It was thus quite apparent that the case land was being used for the benefit of (agricultural) land. In that context the case land was definitely 'land' within the definition of section 2(16) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and not "non-agricultural land" within the definition of section 2(4) of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949. Pre-emption thereof under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was thus quite tenable. Learned lower appellate Court committed an error of law in holding the case land to be non-agricultural land and thereby committed an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 16. In the view of my findings above based on materials on record and legal propositions materially connected therewith, hold that the petitioner was entitled to pre-emption of the case land. The pre-emptee opposite party who was a contiguous land owner like pre-emptor petitioner could have prayed for proportionate pre-emption but since he did not do so his claim of proportionate preemption was barred in terms of the provision of section 96(5)(b) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.
